abstract:
The ML community is rapidly exploring techniques for prompting language models (LMs) and for stacking them into pipelines that solve complex tasks. Unfortunately, existing LM pipelines are typically implemented using hard-coded “prompt templates”, i.e. lengthy strings discovered via trial and error. Toward a more systematic approach for developing and optimizing LM pipelines, we introduce DSPy, a programming model that abstracts LM pipelines as text transformation graphs, i.e. imperative computation graphs where LMs are invoked through declarative modules. DSPy modules are parameterized, meaning they can learn (by creating and collecting demonstrations) how to apply compositions of prompting, finetuning, augmentation, and reasoning techniques. We design a compiler that will optimize any DSPy pipeline to maximize a given metric. We conduct two case studies, showing that succinct DSPy programs can express and optimize sophisticated LM pipelines that reason about math word problems, tackle multi-hop retrieval, answer complex questions, and control agent loops. Within minutes of compiling, a few lines of DSPy allow GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat to self-bootstrap pipelines that outperform standard few-shot prompting (generally by over 25% and 65%, respectively) and pipelines with expert-created demonstrations (by up to 5–46% and 16–40%, respectively). On top of that, DSPy programs compiled to open and relatively small LMs like 770M-parameter T5 and llama2-13b-chat are competitive with approaches that rely on expert-written prompt chains for proprietary GPT-3.5.

DSPy is available at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy.

sections.body: The paper argues that hand-written prompt templates, which are long strings found by trial and error, are brittle and may not transfer across pipelines, LMs, data domains, or inputs. It proposes DSPy, a programming model that expresses LM pipelines as text transformation graphs built from declarative modules, and a compiler that optimizes any DSPy program to maximize a given metric. The section reports that compiled DSPy programs raise simple program quality from 33% to 82% (Sec 6) and from 32% to 46% (Sec 7) for GPT-3.5, and from 9% to 47% (Sec 6) and from 22% to 41% (Sec 7) for llama2-13b-chat. The full evidence is in the two case studies.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Hand-written prompt templates for LM pipelines are brittle, and the paper proposes DSPy to replace them with optimizable modules.

sections.body: This section places DSPy among deep learning frameworks such as Torch and Theano and among in-context learning work. It states that toolkits such as LangChain, Semantic Kernel, and LlamaIndex provide prepackaged chains and agents, but express task-specific behavior through hand-written prompt templates. Prior work applies discrete optimization or reinforcement learning to find prompts, generally for a single LM call. DSPy aims to generalize this to arbitrary pipelines by bootstrapping multi-stage demonstrations from declarative signatures. The section says the paper's focus is empirical: showing that DSPy and its compiler can build LM systems without hand-crafted prompt strings.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Existing toolkits rely on hand-written prompt templates, while DSPy aims to optimize arbitrary multi-stage LM pipelines.

sections.body: A DSPy signature, such as question -> answer, declares what a text transformation must do without specifying how the LM should be prompted. Modules such as `Predict`, `ChainOfThought`, `ProgramOfThought`, `MultiChainComparison`, and `ReAct` implement signatures, and their parameters include the LM, the instructions, and the demonstrations. Retrieval is available through `dspy.Retrieve`, with built-in support for ColBERTv2, Pyserini, and Pinecone. Programs are written define-by-run, in the style of PyTorch. A teleprompter takes a program, a training set, and a metric and returns an optimized program. Labels are assumed only for the final output, and a teacher program can be used to fine-tune a smaller model such as Flan-T5-large.
sections.heading: The DSPy Programming Model
sections.headline: DSPy programs combine typed signatures, parameterized modules, and teleprompters that optimize all modules against a metric.

sections.body: In the first stage, the compiler simulates a teacher program, or the zero-shot program if none is set, on training inputs and keeps multi-stage traces that pass the metric as candidate demonstrations. In the second stage, a teleprompter selects among candidates with search methods such as random search, Optuna, or HyperOpt, or it fine-tunes LM weights with `BootstrapFinetune`. In the third stage, it can change control flow, for example by building an ensemble that runs bootstrapped copies in parallel and reduces their predictions, such as by majority voting. The section says this iteration focuses on demonstrations and that LMs can be highly unreliable, so filtering by the metric is needed.
sections.heading: The DSPy Compiler
sections.headline: The compiler runs three stages: bootstrapping candidate demonstrations, selecting among them, and optimizing control flow.

sections.body: The section sets out three hypotheses. First, hand-crafted prompt strings can be replaced with concise, well-defined modules without reducing quality or expressive power. Second, parameterizing modules and treating prompting as optimization can help DSPy adapt to different LMs and may outperform expert-written prompts. Third, modularity makes it possible to explore complex pipelines with useful performance characteristics or nuanced metrics. The section states that computational efficiency and developer efficiency are other dimensions that it does not focus on. It proposes reporting results as reproducible runs that specify a program and a compilation strategy.
sections.heading: Goals of Evaluation
sections.headline: The evaluation hypothesizes that DSPy can replace hand-written prompts without losing quality, adapt across LMs, and enable richer pipelines.

sections.body: The section evaluates on GSM8K, using 200 training and 300 development question–answer pairs sampled from the official training set, and the 1.3k official test examples for final results. Three programs are compared: a one-step vanilla `Predict`, a two-step `ChainOfThought`, and a ThoughtReflection program that samples five reasoning chains and compares them with `MultiChainComparison`. Compilers include `LabeledFewShot` with `k=8`, bootstrapping with random search, nested bootstrap×2, and ensembles. On GPT-3.5, vanilla development accuracy is 24.0 and bootstrap×2 reaches 64.7. On llama2-13b-chat, vanilla development accuracy is 7.0 and bootstrap×2 reaches 37.3. The section reports development results to avoid overfitting to the test set.
sections.heading: Case Study: Math Word Problems
sections.headline: Compiled DSPy programs improve GPT-3.5 and llama2-13b-chat on math word problems from 4–20% accuracy to 49–88%.

sections.body: The section evaluates multi-hop question answering on HotPotQA in the open-domain fullwiki setting, using a ColBERTv2 retriever over a Wikipedia 2017 abstracts index. Programs include a vanilla few-shot baseline, a `CoT_RAG` program, ReAct, and a multihop program that generates queries over several hops. The multihop program compiled with bootstrap reaches 48.7 dev answer exact match with GPT-3.5, and its ensemble reaches 54.7. A T5-Large model with 770M parameters, fine-tuned with 200 labeled inputs and 800 unlabeled questions, reaches 39.3% answer exact match and 46.0% passage accuracy on dev. The section notes that one test result was measured on 50% of the test set due to cost, and that evaluation methodology varies across studies.
sections.heading: Case Study: Complex Question Answering
sections.headline: On HotPotQA, a multihop program compiled with ensembling reaches 54.7 dev answer exact match with GPT-3.5.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes DSPy as a programming model with three abstractions: signatures, modules, and teleprompters. The authors say they have maintained open-source versions for close to a year and have built many programs that DSPy compiled into high-quality systems, spanning information extraction to low-resource synthetic data generation. They leave reporting these tasks under controlled conditions to future work to keep the paper's scope reasonable. The section argues that the expressive power lies in text transformation graphs, where composable modules and teleprompters work together with LMs. It adds no new quantitative results beyond the two case studies.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: DSPy supports rapid development of effective systems with small LMs, and wider task reporting is deferred to future work.

sections.body: The appendix gives signatures written as Python classes with explicit instructions, an example information retrieval dataset generator, and a work-in-progress option to type output fields as `bool`, `int`, `float`, `list`, or `dict`. Appendix B compares DSPy with LangChain and LlamaIndex. In an informal study from late September 2023, the authors found 50 strings exceeding 1000 characters in the LangChain codebase and none in DSPy, along with 12 `prompts.py` files and 42 `prompt.py` files. The LangChain Program-Aided Language Model chain uses a template 3982 characters long with 8 math word problems. Appendix F shows prompts that DSPy generated automatically for GSM8K and HotPotQA.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers advanced signatures, a comparison with LangChain and LlamaIndex, and long prompts from existing libraries and DSPy.
